newsitem.title: USA: Stocks jump on relief at jobs report.
newsitem.headline: Stocks jump on relief at jobs report.

text.p: Stocks shot up Friday after the August U.S. employment report eased Wall Street's worst fears about a sharp rise in interest rates.

Although the report was slightly stronger than expected, it failed to convince markets that the economy was overheating enough to force the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates by half a percentage point at its Sept. 24 policy meeting.
Just after 1 p.m. EDT, the Dow Jones industrial average was up 52.53 points at 5,659.49. The more than 50-point rise led the New York Stock Exchange to impose curbs on computerized trading.
In the broader market, advancing issues led decliners by a 15-6 margin on volume of 202 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index gained 11.94 points to 1,137.60.

The Labour Department said non-farm payrolls for August rose by 250,000, a shade ahead of a consensus forecast of 244,000. Average hourly wages grew by 0.5 percent, compared to a forecast of 0.3 percent growth.

"Now that the numbers have come in fairly decent, it looks more like a 25 basis point (one-quarter percentage point) move," said Hildegard Zagorski, market analyst at Prudential Securities, referring to the likely size of the Fed's expected rate hike. "These numbers wouldn't justify a 50 basis point (one-half percentage point) move."
A bit more surprising was a steep drop in the nation's employment rate, to 5.1 percent from July's 5.4 percent. Economists had called for a drop to 5.3 percent.
That figure was not enough, however, to trouble a stock market that sold off heavily at the end of Thursday's session, apparently bracing for the worst.
"The hurricane that was expected has apparently passed by," said Alan Ackerman, market strategist at Fahnestock & Co. "We've backed away from the fear of a 50-basis-point move."

However, analysts warned that interest rates remain a key focus for stocks and said an extended rally was very unlikely unless Treasury securities gained enough momentum to push long-term yields back below 7 percent.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond mustered a rally of half a point after a dramatic drop in the first minutes after release of the payrolls report. The yield, which moves in the opposite direction to price, fell to 7.11 percent from 7.15 percent at Thursday's close.
Analysts also said that with the worst case scenario apparently averted, investors would likely refocus on some of the fundamentals beyond the interest rate outlook.

"I think there's a shift here," said Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist at Dean Witter. "If the economy is doing fine, I think people are going to start to buying on earnings instead of the interest rate outlook."
Investors got their first major dose of third-quarter earnings pre-announcements late Thursday and early Friday and several individual issues suffered steep losses as a result.
Verity Inc. fell 11-1/8 to 13 after it said it expected to post a fiscal first-quarter loss of $1.3 million. The company also said it expected revenues to decline from fourth-quarter levels.
Workgroup Technology Corp. tumbled 7-7/8, or more than 50 percent, to 7-1/8, after saying it may lose money in its second, third and fourth quarters.

Gap Inc., which was hit with severe selling pressure on Thursday after reporting flat August same-store sales, rebounded a bit, rising 1-1/4 to 30-1/4. The stock, which was once again the NYSE's most active, was upgraded by several investment firms this morning.
The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks rose 5.90 points to 655.34.
